title: Foundations: Heartland Rock - The Complete Guide
summary: What Heartland Rock is, where it came from, and how its songs work.
body:
Heartland Rock songs: Heartland rock sings the American middle: factory towns, highways, and small dreams, with Springsteen's poetry, Mellencamp's twang, and Petty's jangle. Working-class anthems with big choruses.

History: Bruce Springsteen's Born to Run (1975) and Born in the U.S.A. (1984), Bob Seger, Tom Petty, and John Mellencamp defined the sound: rock and roll about ordinary American lives.

How the songs work: Heartland Rock favors the keys of G, D, A, E. Common forms include Verse-chorus with a harmonica or sax break; Story verses, singalong chorus. Players should master rickenbacker jangle: bright 12-string chime first, then harmonica fills between vocal lines. Capo 2 for jangly open-string drive.

summary: An original Heartland Rock study in D drilling harmonica fills between vocal lines.

title: Born in the U.S.A. - Heartland Rock Song Study
summary: Harmonic blueprint and playing guide for Born in the U.S.A. by Bruce Springsteen (1984).
body:
Born in the U.S.A. — Bruce Springsteen, 1984. Misread as patriotic; it's a Vietnam veteran's lament.

HARMONIC BLUEPRINT (study chart, key of A):
A | E | F#m | C#m

This study chart uses the 'Jangle I–V–vi–iii' progression, the Heartland Rock workhorse, to map how songs like this move. Form: verse-chorus with a harmonica or sax break. Listen for the e street lift: band kicks in on the chorus — it is the fingerprint of the style.

TO PLAY IT: set your tempo to the Heartland Rock pocket, voice the chords cleanly, and let the e street lift: band kicks in on the chorus. Capo 2 for jangly open-string drive. (Song facts: title/artist/year are documented public records; the chart is an original study arrangement.)
